newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - U.S. buying supports market.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - U.S. buying supports market.

text.p: Asian crude prices are expected to remain steady this week, as the movement of barrels to the U.S. takes out some length from the regional market, traders said on Monday.
At least one million barrels of heavy sweet Indonesian Widuri crude, loading at the end of this month were heard to be heading to the U.S. Gulf Coast for refining, traders said.

The relative weakness of Asian crudes, due to lacklustre demand from Japan and China coupled with the rise in West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude levels have opened the arbitrage window to the U.S., they said.

"The backwardation in WTI is quite narrow, and as traders have a good idea of the latest official Indonesian Crude Price (ICP), they would try to take barrels to the U.S.", said a trader at a major oil company
In the last month, Asian crudes have been languishing under an oversupplied market.
Traders said traditional increase in Japanese demand, for summer stockpiling, has not emerged as expected.
They said mild weather in Japan, as well as greater use of nuclear and natural gas for electricity generation, has deterred Japanese utilities from buying more heavy crudes for direct burning.
China had also covered the bulk of its crude requirements with West African cargoes, limiting its demand for Minas and Widuri, traders said.

But they said Asian crude prices may have reached a floor, as the arbitrage window for West African crudes moving East is currently unworkable. They said this would forced buyers to look at regional crudes in Asia.

Although some Japanese traders are aggressive, selling June Minas cargoes at low premiums of 15 cents over the ICP to dispose of barrels, other sellers are holding out for ICP +30, expecting and upturn in prices.
But continuing weak margins in Asia could undermine any increase in crude buying over the next week, traders said.
On Friday, gasoil in Singapore broke the $25 support level, trading below that for the first time in nine months.
Japanese refiners are also having high stocks of middle distillates, reducing their need for crude imports.
July trading for Oman and Abu Dhabi crudes should start by this week. But the weak margins and an overhang in June supplies of Middle East crudes are likely to bear down on the July market.
A Japanese trader was offering July Oman at a discount of five cents to the official MPM, but found very limited buying interest from refiners.
The only support for Oman could come from the lack of July cargoes of Yemeni Masila, the closest alternative crude to Oman, traders said.
Discussion for the third quarter term price between Yemen and its crude buyers are underway, and are expected to last a few weeks.
Spot sellers of Masila would therefore be unwilling to offer July cargoes until the third quarter term price is fixed, traders said.
